stages.name: Policies for international competitiveness
stages.title: Policies for international competitiveness
stages.sub: You can identify how governments try to raise competitiveness and judge how well those measures actually work.

steps.q: A government wants firms to produce more efficiently in the long run, so it spends on better roads, ports and worker training. What kind of policy is this, using tools you already know?
steps.hint: Think about which tool box roads, ports and training come from.

steps.q: Better roads mean goods move faster and cheaper, and trained workers produce more per hour worked. What happens to the cost of making each unit of output?
steps.hint: If transport and labour are both more efficient, does output cost more or less per unit?
steps.pre: So these measures work by helping to

steps.q: A country's currency has been strong, making its exports pricier abroad. The government leans on its central bank to help push the exchange rate down. Alongside supply-side spending, is this also aimed at making exports cheaper for foreigners to buy?
steps.right: Yes, both aim to make exports more competitive
steps.wrong: No, only supply-side spending affects export prices
steps.hint: A weaker currency and lower unit costs both change how expensive exports look to foreign buyers.

steps.q: New infrastructure and training schemes are announced today. Will firms' costs fall tomorrow, or only after roads are built and workers are trained years later?
steps.hint: Building a port or retraining a workforce takes time to complete, not days.
steps.pre: So one problem with these policies is

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: The government cuts firms' taxes and eases regulation to lower costs and boost competitiveness. But this also cuts tax revenue and weakens workplace protections. Could this clash with the government's other goals, like a balanced budget or fair working conditions?
steps.right: Yes, it could work against other goals
steps.wrong: No, competitiveness policy cannot affect other goals
steps.hint: Lower taxes and lighter regulation have knock-on effects beyond just competitiveness.

steps.q: To check whether all this spending and currency action actually worked, you compare a country's unit labour costs with its trading partners' over several years, using a measure you already know. Does simply announcing policies guarantee competitiveness has improved?
steps.right: No, it must be checked against actual data
steps.hint: Policies are aims; the measure tells you what really happened to costs relative to other countries.
